paragraphs.text: At the edge of the forest, the Three Little Pigs built houses and waited to be admired. The first used straw, the second wood, and the third enough bricks to make him feel sensible. None paid much attention to what lay beneath the walls.

Across the creek, G. Wolf lived in a gray stone cottage with a level floor and a stove that drew well. In the evening he made fish soup with dill. Mira and Tansy, two young pigs from the market, sometimes smelled it on their way home. They knew very little about their neighbor. They knew a great deal about wolves in stories.
The first strong wind pulled the straw house apart. Its owner stood among the scattered bundles with straw in his ears.
“G. Wolf blew it down,” he announced.
“I heard him laughing,” said his brother, who had heard the wind.

The Third Little Pig hesitated. Then he saw the neighbors waiting for him to nod, and nodded. A wicked wolf was easier to explain than a weak house. By supper they had told the story often enough to stop mentioning the weather.
The pigs printed a poster. Its wolf had red eyes and a mouth large enough to swallow a roof. They nailed it beside the market scales, where everyone had to wait.
Mira read it to Tansy. Tansy repeated it to the next pig in line. Neither had seen the house fall, but both began watching the creek path.

The baker no longer called Wolf over for a chat. Children were pulled away from his gate. The same paper that said he was dangerous told the young pigs to report anything suspicious. It was a small sheet. It managed to stand between a great many neighbors.
One morning before the market opened, Wolf packed his pot, his spoon, and his dried dill. He left the cottage empty and followed the creek until it became a river, then followed the river to the sea.
On the rocky shore he could hear water instead of whispers. He made no houses fall there. Back in the valley, the poster stayed on its tree. It no longer needed him to be present.
Heavy rain softened the ground beneath the wooden house. One corner sank; the rest followed it sideways into the mud.
“He has done it again,” said the Second Little Pig.
“From the sea?” someone asked.
“Why else would he have run away?”

The pigs bought a printing press. Their newspaper made flight into proof and mud into a detail too dull to print. Young pigs learned which questions earned praise. Questions about wolves were welcome. Questions about foundations were less so.
Then a crack opened in the brick house. Its walls were heavy; its footing was poor. The Third Little Pig put a picture over the crack, but the picture would not lie flat.

The brothers agreed that three accidents could hardly be an accident. They moved into Wolf's cottage, with its good light and straight walls. It still belonged to Wolf. That did not prevent the pigs from sleeping in it.
For a little while, owning the loudest story seemed almost as useful as owning the house.
Whispers began about the pigs living in a wolf's house. The brothers decided the valley needed its villain back where everyone could see him.

They found Wolf on the shore. He was old, and there were three of them. They brought him home to the cracked brick house and required him to build cottages for the young pigs. He measured the ground, laid firm stones, and showed the workers how to use a level.
“Look what we have built,” the brothers told the newspaper. Wolf went on measuring. The new cottages were sound. The story attached to them was not.
Story Fox arrived while Wolf was setting out another foundation. The watch list had a place for wolves and no place for foxes. She studied the poster, then the unattended lunch baskets.
By noon, three portions of cheese had disappeared into her mouth.

Mira and Tansy had been carrying bricks; neither saw her take it. “It must be Wolf,” they said. The brothers agreed, and promised tighter rules. Fox licked her whiskers behind the baskets. Nobody searched beneath the red tail.
Fox heard a new name in the work gangs: the Three Little Wolves. She carried it to the cottage by the creek.
“Such a fine wolf's house,” she told the brothers. “The young pigs say you have become quite at home in it.”
“We are pigs,” said the First Little Pig.
“Naturally.” Fox looked up at the stonework. “Though a house can tell a story of its own.”

That night the brothers looked at their comfortable walls as if the walls had grown fur. They wanted a building that would settle who they were. Fox wanted another reason to stay near the lunch baskets.
“A palace,” said the Third Little Pig. “On the hill. With a tower.”

Fox suggested books. Famous palaces had plans, she explained; a truly important palace ought to have important plans. The pigs ordered wagons of them. Wolf turned one upside-down volume the right way up and went to examine the hill.

Mira and Tansy carried stone. Wolf laid out the rooms. Between the windows they built shelves for books about foundations, bridges, roofs, and water. The pigs left the shelves open so that visitors would admire the collection. They had bought the books to be seen. They did not think very hard about being read.
The brothers assigned the young pigs to separate jobs. Each answered to a different overseer; their breaks rarely overlapped.

Tansy found a book of bridges. A little drawing put a support beneath the middle of a long plank. It looked almost disappointingly simple. He fetched a scrap of wood and laid it across two stones to see why anyone had bothered to draw it. Each time he found his place, someone called him away. By the fourth errand, he could remember the bridge but not quite how its parts worked together.

Mira took down the foundations book. One drawing showed water gathering against a wall; another showed it running away through a shallow channel. She recognized the first picture. Her own doorstep looked like that whenever it rained.

“Where would the water go here?” she murmured, tracing the channel with a dusty hoof. The overseer called for four different errands before a whole page could be read. The picture was memorable. The reason for its details was not yet clear.
At lunch Wolf brought his old pot up the hill and shared fish soup with Mira. There was a little dill left.
“You kept it all the way to the sea?” she asked.
“And back.”

She held the warm bowl while he wiped mortar from his sleeve. It was difficult to fit this tired builder inside the mouth drawn on the poster. Wolf did not ask her to decide anything about him before finishing her soup.
Mira cut a channel that looked rather like the picture. She had missed how steeply it needed to fall. Her bucketful crept a little way, stopped, and soaked the bricks.
She moved one muddy hoof out of the puddle. “I haven't understood it yet.”
The work bell rang before she could try again. She put the book back with a strip of grass marking the unfinished page.
The brothers brought the newspaper to the worksite. Its headline congratulated them on their palace. Beneath it, the familiar wolf watched from the familiar drawing.

Mira and Tansy read the instruction to obey their elders. Old words could still make them lower their voices, even here among stones they had carried themselves. The pigs left the paper where the workers would pass it again.
Tansy set his plank on two end stones and piled bricks over the gap. He had copied the outline of the bridge without giving its middle enough support. The wood bowed; a brick slid into the dirt.
He took the load off slowly. The picture had made sense while he looked at it. Making it stand up was another matter. He kept the book open until the bell made him close it.
At last the roof was finished and the scaffolding came down. The tower could be seen from the market. The brothers climbed the steps in order of importance, disagreeing quietly about the order.
Inside, the books occupied the walls intended for portraits. Mira looked for the foundations volume; Tansy looked for the bridge drawing. Their unfinished thoughts were inside those covers.
“These were tools,” said the Third Little Pig. “Now we need the space. Take the books away.”
“A memorable opening ceremony,” said Fox from a window ledge.
Mira opened her mouth, then shut it. Tansy watched the floor. Neither could yet point to a successful trial of their own. The familiar instruction to obey came more readily than an answer.
The Third Little Pig repeated his order, louder this time.
The books went behind locked doors. The brothers chose places for their portraits and sent Wolf back to the brick house with tomorrow's building list.

They returned to his cottage by the creek for supper. The newspaper would describe the palace as another triumph. Fox watched them go. She had obtained her tower full of books; she had not obtained readers able to keep it.

Mira stopped inside the doorway before going home. Through the cupboard wire she could see a blue spine with a drawing of water on it. Beyond her reach, its gilt arrow pointed downhill. At her own doorstep, rainwater gathered in the same old place.

qa.question: Why did the straw house fall?
qa.answer: Wind pulled the weak straw house apart. The accusation against Wolf did not change the physical cause of its collapse.

qa.question: Where was Wolf when the wooden house fell?
qa.answer: Wolf had already left for the shore when the wooden house fell. Rain weakened its footing into mud while he was away.

qa.question: Who owned the cottage when the pigs moved in?
qa.answer: The cottage still belonged to Wolf. The pigs occupied it after their brick house cracked; occupying it did not make them its owners.

qa.question: Who took the cheese?
qa.answer: Story Fox took the cheese. She ate the three portions while attention was directed toward wolves.

qa.question: Who did the pigs blame for the cheese theft?
qa.answer: The pigs blamed Wolf for the missing cheese. Their accusation contradicted the recorded theft by Story Fox.

qa.question: Did Mira see who took the cheese?
qa.answer: Mira did not see the theft and had no direct observation of who took the cheese. The pigs continued to blame Wolf.

qa.question: Could the young pigs reach the books during construction?
qa.answer: The shelves were open, so the young pigs could reach the books. The pigs displayed their collection without preventing workers from reading it.

qa.question: Did Mira's drain work?
qa.answer: Mira's drain failed its trial. The channel lacked enough fall to carry the water away.

qa.question: Did Tansy's bridge work?
qa.answer: Tansy's bridge failed its trial. The plank lacked enough support for the test load of bricks.

qa.question: Did the young pigs act together at the opening?
qa.answer: Neither young pig spoke against the order. Neither could point to a successful trial that gave them a practical reason to defend the books.

qa.question: What became of the palace?
qa.answer: The pigs kept the palace and locked away its books. Without successful practical learning, the young pigs did not resist the removal order.

qa.question: Did Wolf get his cottage back?
qa.answer: Wolf did not recover his cottage. The pigs still occupied it, and he remained required to sleep in their brick house.
